Plant ash, especially from saltwort, which was used to make soap.
For liquid–vapor equilibrium, what relationship does the Clausius–Clapeyron equation describe?
How equilibrium vapor pressure changes with temperature, in terms of the enthalpy of vaporization under the equation's approximations.
What is the difference between physisorption and chemisorption?
Physisorption is weak van der Waals attraction; chemisorption involves the formation of chemical bonds between adsorbate and surface
Which radioactive element did Marie Curie name after her homeland?
What is a London dispersion force?
A temporary attractive force arising from instantaneous dipoles induced in adjacent atoms or molecules
What is Avogadro's number and what does it represent?
6.022 × 10²³; it is the number of atoms, molecules, or ions in one mole of a substance.
What is the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid?
In water, a strong acid such as HCl ionizes essentially completely. A weak acid such as acetic acid ionizes only partly and reaches an equilibrium with its conjugate base.
Why can two enantiomers of a chiral molecule have different biological effects?
Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images. Biological targets such as enzymes are also chiral, so the two forms may bind or react differently.
What is the Born–Haber cycle used to calculate?
The lattice energy of an ionic compound, using Hess's law.
What is the difference between SN1 and SN2 reactions?
SN1 is unimolecular (two steps, via a carbocation); SN2 is bimolecular (one step, with inversion).
What is the shape of a water molecule (H₂O)?
Bent (V-shaped), with a bond angle of about 104.5°.
The Statue of Liberty was a shiny reddish-brown when it was built. What turned it green?
Its copper skin reacted with air and moisture, forming a green coating called patina.
Rose water, used in many Arab sweets and perfumes, is traditionally made from rose petals by which separation process?
Distillation: steam carries off the rose oils, then cools and condenses into rose water.
In 1940, to hide two Nobel Prize gold medals from the Nazis, chemist George de Hevesy dissolved them in which liquid?
Aqua regia, a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids.
Most metals look silvery, but gold is yellow. Which famous physics theory is needed to explain its colour?
Einstein's relativity: relativistic effects on gold's fast-moving electrons make it absorb blue light.
Selenium is named after the Greek word for the Moon. Which element directly below it in the periodic table is named after the Earth?
The word 'ammonia' goes back to an ancient Egyptian god, because ammonium salt was collected near his temple in the Libyan desert. Which god?
Which orange-red molecule in henna leaves stains skin and hair by binding to their keratin?
Amman-born chemist Omar Yaghi shared the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for building porous crystals that can even pull drinking water from desert air. What are these materials called?
When you stand in sunlight, I copy your outline on the ground but have no face. What am I?
What disappears every time you stand up?
I have a zipper for a mouth, carry books in my belly, and ride on your back. What am I?
I am always coming but never arrive. What am I?
I have a spout but no mouth and a lid but no head. Fill me with hot water and leaves, and I'll pour you a cup. What am I?
What goes all the way around a house but never moves?
Call out in an empty valley, and I may repeat your words without a mouth. What am I?
I am tall when I'm young and short when I'm old. What am I?
Layla points to a boy and says, “His mother is the only daughter of my mother.” Layla has no sisters. Who is the boy to Layla?
I drift across the sky without wings and can release rain without eyes. What am I?
I have no life, but I can die. I have no lungs, but I need air. What am I?
Who is your maternal uncle's sister but not your aunt?
What has a thumb and four fingers but no flesh or bone?
What goes up and down but never moves?
What walks on four legs in the morning, two in the afternoon, and three in the evening?
What is so fragile that even saying its name breaks it?
The more of this there is, the less you see. What is it?
Which is heavier: a kilo of cotton or a kilo of iron?
Neither. They both weigh one kilo.
What has to be broken before you can use it?
If you have me, you want to share me. If you share me, you no longer have me. What am I?
I have hands but can't clap, and a face but can't smile. What am I?
I am full of holes but can hold water. What am I?
What goes up but never comes down?
The more of them you take, the more you leave behind. What are they?
What has one eye but cannot see?
I have a neck but no head. What am I?
I have legs but cannot walk. What am I?
What is always in front of you but cannot be seen?
The more you use me the smaller I get. What am I?
A bar of soap (or a pencil/candle)
What has teeth but cannot bite?
I'm lighter than a feather, yet the strongest person can't hold me for more than a few minutes. What am I?
Each side of a square café table seats one guest. If two such tables are pushed together along one full side, how many guests can sit around the exposed sides?
I have a spine but no bones, and leaves but no branches. What am I?
I show cities, mountains and rivers on a flat surface, but no one can live in my cities or swim in my rivers. What am I?
A little girl wears seventy dresses, and whoever peels them off ends up in tears. What is she?
Using the numbers 2, 3 and 4 exactly once, and only addition and multiplication, how can you make 14?
What can you hold in your right hand but not your left?
I turn a blank wall into a window onto another place, but when I am unplugged the wall becomes plain again. What am I?
What gets bigger the more you take from it?
Some months have 30 days and some have 31. How many have 28?
All 12: every month has at least 28 days.
There's a green house. Inside it is a white house, inside that a red house, and inside the red house live lots of little black babies. What is it?
You have 3 stoves, 3 gas burners, and 3 electric burners — but only one match. Which do you light first?
I may have many branches in a city, but none grows leaves. People visit them to deposit or withdraw money. What am I?
I'm taken from a mine and shut inside a wooden case that I never leave, yet almost everyone uses me. What am I?
What can travel around the world while staying in a corner?
What number gives the same answer whether you add 3 to it or multiply it by 3?
The person who makes it, sells it. The person who buys it never uses it. The person who uses it doesn't know they're using it. What is it?
A coffin (a burial shroud also fits).
What is the smallest positive number that leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4, remainder 4 when divided by 5, and remainder 5 when divided by 6?
Place me to the right of a whole number and its value becomes ten times larger. Place me to its left and its value stays the same. What digit am I?
In a non-leap year, January 1 is a Monday. What day of the week is March 1?
You have weights of 1, 3, 9, and 27 units and a two-pan balance. Weights may be placed on either pan. How can you balance an object weighing 20 units?
Put the object with the 9- and 1-unit weights on one pan, and the 27- and 3-unit weights on the other: 20+9+1 = 27+3
The sun gives birth to me from the sea, and the sea kills me if I go back to it. What am I?
Salt: the sun dries seawater to leave it behind, and it dissolves when it goes back into water.

Find the three distinct digits: 571 has one correct and placed; 183 has one correct but misplaced; 120 has two correct, both misplaced; 765 has none; 248 has one correct but misplaced. What is the code?

A, B and C are Truth, Lie and Random in an unknown order. Truth always answers truthfully, Lie always falsely, and Random may answer yes or no arbitrarily. They understand the questions and know each other’s types. Using three yes/no questions, identify all three.

Use N(Q): “If I asked you Q, would you say yes?” For a non-random person, N(Q) answers Q truthfully. Ask A N(“Is B Random?”). If yes, choose X=C; if no, choose X=B. X is certainly non-random: if A is Random both others are safe; otherwise its normalized answer excludes Random. Ask X N(“Is A Random?”). If yes, A is Random; if no, the unchosen member of B and C is Random. Finally ask X N(“Are you Truth?”). If yes, X is Truth; if no, X is Lie. The remaining non-random person has the opposite type.
What is the smallest positive integer that is divisible by 7 and leaves remainder 1 when divided by each of 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6?

Five runners are Amal, Basel, Dana, Hadi, and Lina. Dana finishes immediately after Amal; Hadi is last; Amal finishes before Lina; Lina finishes before Basel; and Basel is not second. What is the finishing order?
An 8-liter container is full, while unmarked 5-liter and 3-liter containers are empty. By pouring only until a container is full or empty, how can you split the water into two equal 4-liter portions?
I am a three-digit number whose digits increase by 2 from left to right. Reversing my digits makes the number 396 larger, and my digits add to 15. What number am I?

Ten discs of different sizes are stacked largest to smallest on one of three pegs. Move them to another peg, moving one top disc at a time and never placing a larger disc on a smaller one. What is the minimum number of moves?
1,023. To move n discs, move n−1 aside, move the largest, then move n−1 onto it: T(n)=2T(n−1)+1, with T(1)=1. Thus T(10)=2¹⁰−1.
A, B, and C are each either always truthful or always lying. A says, “B is truthful.” B says, “C is lying.” C says, “A and B are different types.” Which type is each person?
A and B are truthful; C is lying
There are two sisters: one gives birth to the other, who in turn gives birth to the first. Who are they?
A tank contains 100 fish. Ten die but remain in the tank. Fifteen other fish are removed, and five of those are returned. Counting living and dead fish, how many are now in the tank?
90 fish: the ten dead fish still count, so 100 − 15 + 5 = 90.
What is the smallest odd positive integer that has exactly six positive divisors?
Thirty white horses on a red hill: first they champ, then they stamp, then they stand still. What are they?
I'm black when you buy me, red when you use me, and grey when you throw me away. What am I?

Gear A has 12 teeth and drives gear B with 18 teeth. B shares an axle with gear C, which has 10 teeth and drives gear D with 25 teeth. If A turns 15 times clockwise, how many times and in which direction does D turn?
If there are 6 apples and you take away 4, how many apples do YOU have?
I run but never walk, I have a mouth but never talk, a head but never weep, and a bed but never sleep. What am I?
What letter comes next: O, T, T, F, F, S, S, E, …?
N, for Nine: these are the first letters of One, Two, Three… Eight.
What moves forward only when it's hit on the head?
A lily pad doubles in size every day. It takes 48 days to cover the entire pond. How long did it take to cover half the pond?
47 days. On day 47 it covered half — then doubled on day 48 to cover it all.
A girl has as many brothers as sisters. Each brother has half as many brothers as sisters. How many children are there in total?
7 children: 4 girls and 3 boys. Each girl has 3 brothers and 3 sisters. Each boy has 2 brothers and 4 sisters.
You overtake the person in 2nd place in a race. What place are you in now?
2nd place. You took their position — you did not overtake 1st place.
In this puzzle, each egg needs exactly five minutes once placed in boiling water. A large pot keeps boiling normally with five eggs in it. If all five go in together, when are they ready?
After five minutes: the cooking happens simultaneously.
Lina, Sami, and Noor each chose a different drink: tea, coffee, or juice. Sami chose coffee, Noor did not choose juice, and Lina did not choose tea. Who chose each drink?
Noor chose tea, Sami chose coffee, and Lina chose juice. Once coffee is assigned to Sami, Noor's only allowed drink is tea, leaving juice for Lina.
A doctor gives you three pills and tells you to take one every half hour. How long until you have taken them all?
One hour: the first now, the second after 30 minutes and the third after 60 minutes.
A rider arrives in town on Friday, stays three days, and leaves on Friday. How?
An electric train is travelling north and the wind is blowing west. Which way does its smoke blow?
Nowhere: an electric train gives off no smoke.
A box contains two red balls and one blue ball. Without looking, how many balls must you take to guarantee having a red ball?
Two. At most one drawn ball can be blue.
Mona's father has five daughters: Nana, Nene, Nini and Nono. What is the fifth daughter's name?
A light starts off. You press a switch five times; each press reverses its state. Is it on or off at the end?
On. Odd-numbered presses turn it on; even-numbered presses turn it off.
When I was 6 my sister was half my age. Now I am 70. How old is my sister?
67. She was 3 when I was 6 — so she is always 3 years younger than me.
A rooster lays an egg on a roof peak. Which way does the egg roll?
A farmer has 17 sheep and all but 9 die. How many sheep are left?
A two-digit number has digits that add to 11. Reversing its digits makes the number 27 greater. What is the original number?
47. If the tens digit is a and the ones digit is b, then a+b=11 and 9(b−a)=27, so b−a=3. Thus a=4 and b=7.
A three-digit vault code has distinct digits. The first digit is twice the third, the middle digit is one greater than the third, and all three digits add to 13. What is the code?
643. Let the third digit be t. The digits are 2t, t+1, and t, so 4t+1=13 and t=3.
Is 8% of 50 the same as 50% of 8?
Yes, both equal 4. In general, x% of y always equals y% of x.
What is the sum of all integers from 1 to 100?
Three boxes are labelled 'Apples', 'Oranges' and 'Mixed', but every label is wrong. You may take one fruit from one box without looking inside. Which box should you pick from to fix all the labels?
The box labelled 'Mixed'. It must hold only one kind of fruit, so whatever you pull out tells you what it holds, and the other two labels follow.
You drive 60 miles to a shop at a constant 20 mph and return along the same 60-mile route at 60 mph, with no stops. What is your average speed for the whole journey?
30 mph. The 120 miles take 3 + 1 = 4 hours, so 120 ÷ 4 = 30.
Among 4, 6 and 8, which number equals the sum of its positive divisors smaller than itself?
6: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. For 4 the sum is 3, and for 8 it is 7.
I am a father. Another man’s only son is my son’s father. Who am I to that other man?
His son. The man's only son is my son's father — meaning I am that son.

A treasure is in exactly one of three boxes. Box 1 says, “The treasure is in Box 2.” Box 2 says, “The treasure is not in Box 2.” Box 3 says, “The treasure is not in Box 1.” Exactly one note is true. Which box holds the treasure?
Box 1. If the treasure is there, only Box 2's note is true. Putting it in Box 2 or Box 3 makes two notes true.
A man builds a house with all four walls facing south. A bear walks past. What colour is the bear?
White. Only at the North Pole can every wall face south, so it's a polar bear.
On a 24-hour digital clock, 12:21 is palindromic. What is the next palindromic time, and how many minutes later is it?
Which three consecutive positive integers have the same sum and product?

Four cards show A, D, 4 and 7. Each has an English letter on one side and a number on the other. To test “If the letter is a vowel (A, E, I, O or U), the number is even,” which cards must you turn over?
A and 7. Turn A to check for an even number, and 7 to make sure there is not a vowel on its other side. D and 4 cannot disprove the rule.
A dealer offers you an ancient coin stamped '44 BC'. Why must it be fake?
Nobody in 44 BC knew they were living 'before Christ'; that dating system was invented centuries later.
Three talks—AI, Design, and History—must fill slots 1, 2, and 3. AI is before Design, Design is not in slot 3, and History is not in slot 1. What is the schedule?
Slot 1: AI; slot 2: Design; slot 3: History. No other ordering satisfies all three constraints.
A cube is painted on all six faces and cut into 27 equal smaller cubes. How many small cubes have exactly two painted faces?
12. Each of the cube's 12 edges has one non-corner small cube, and each such cube has exactly two painted faces.
In a class of 30 students, 18 study Arabic, 14 study English, and 5 study neither language. How many study both Arabic and English?
7. Twenty-five students study at least one language, so the overlap is 18 + 14 − 25 = 7.
Exactly two of four lamps A, B, C, and D are lit. A and B are in opposite states, C is in the same state as A, and D is off. Which lamps are lit?
A and C. If A were off, only B would be lit, contradicting the condition that exactly two lamps are lit. Therefore A and C are on, while B and D are off.

A car is placed uniformly behind one of three doors. You choose one. The host knows its location, always opens an unchosen goat door, and always offers a switch to the other closed door. Does always switching or always staying win more often?
Switching wins with probability 2/3; staying wins with probability 1/3. Switching wins exactly when the initial choice was wrong.
100 lockers are all closed. Person 1 opens all; person 2 toggles every 2nd; person 3 toggles every 3rd... Which lockers remain open after all 100 people?
The perfect squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100. Only perfect squares have an odd number of divisors, so they end up open.

In an idealized two-child model, each child is independently equally likely to be a boy or girl. A family is selected at random from those with at least one boy, without inspecting a particular child. What is the probability of two boys?
1/3. The equally likely ordered possibilities remaining are boy-boy, boy-girl and girl-boy.
A robot travels 1 metre, then half a metre, then a quarter, and keeps halving each new distance forever. What total distance does the sequence approach?
2 metres. If S = 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + …, then S/2 = 1/2 + 1/4 + …; subtracting gives S/2 = 1.
An ant sits on one corner of a 1×1×1 cube. What is the shortest path along the surface to the opposite corner?
√5 ≈ 2.236. Unfold two faces into a flat 1×2 rectangle — the straight line across is √(1² + 2²) = √5.

Exactly one of two paths is safe. Two guards know which one: one always answers truthfully and the other always lies. Both know the other’s rule. What single yes/no question to either guard lets you choose the safe path?
Ask: “Would the other guard say the left path is safe?” If yes, go right; if no, go left. Either guard gives the opposite of the truth about the left path.
Two fathers and two sons go fishing. They each catch exactly one fish, yet only three fish are caught in total. How?
There are only three people: a grandfather, a father, and a son. The father counts as both a father and a son.
If a plane crashes exactly on the border between two countries, in which country do they bury the survivors?
Use exactly eight copies of the digit 8 to make 1000. You may join adjacent 8s into numbers such as 88 or 888, and use addition only. What expression works?
How can a man go eight days without sleep and still feel fine?
He sleeps at night; he just doesn't sleep during the days.
A statement says, “This statement is false.” In classical two-valued logic, what contradiction follows from assuming it is true?
If it is true, what it asserts must hold, so it is false. Assuming it false likewise makes its assertion true; no consistent classical truth assignment works.
A snail is at the bottom of a 10-metre well. Each day it climbs 3 metres and each night slips back 2 metres. How many days does it take to escape?
8 days. After seven full days and nights, the snail is at 7 m. On day 8 it climbs to 10 m and escapes, so it does not slide back that night.

Three switches outside a room control three initially off incandescent bulbs inside. The bulbs become warm when on and remain detectably warm briefly after switching off. You may safely inspect light and residual warmth, but enter only once. How can you match switches to bulbs?
Leave switch 1 on long enough to warm its bulb, then turn it off. Turn switch 2 on and enter promptly. Lit = 2; unlit but warm = 1; unlit and cool = 3.

100 prisoners may agree on a plan before isolation. A lamp starts off. One prisoner visits its room at a time and may change the lamp. Everyone is selected repeatedly without limit. How can one prisoner eventually know with certainty that all have visited?

Choose one counter. Each other prisoner signals once: on the first visit when they have not yet signalled and find the lamp off, they turn it on. On all other visits they leave it unchanged. Only the counter turns it off, counting each such event. At 99 signals, all have visited. Repeated selection guarantees eventual completion.
Each term describes the runs of identical digits in the preceding term. What follows 1, 11, 21, 1211, 111221?
312211. Read 111221 as three 1s, two 2s and one 1; writing those counts followed by their digits gives 31 22 11.

Twelve balls are labelled 1–12. Exactly one has a different mass; the other eleven have the same mass. You do not know whether the odd ball is heavier or lighter. Give three balance-scale weighings and a complete rule to identify the odd ball and its type.

Weigh left versus right: (1) 5,7,8,9 vs 6,10,11,12; (2) 2,3,4,6 vs 5,10,11,12; (3) 1,4,9,10 vs 2,6,7,12. Record L if left is heavier, R if right is heavier, and = if balanced. Heavy-ball signatures: 1:==L; 2:=LR; 3:=L=; 4:=LL; 5:LR=; 6:RLR; 7:L=R; 8:L==; 9:L=L; 10:RRL; 11:RR=; 12:RRR. A matching signature identifies a heavy ball. Otherwise swap L and R in your result; the matching signature identifies a light ball. All 24 signatures are different.
You have two ropes, each taking exactly 1 hour to burn, but with non-uniform burning rates. How do you measure exactly 45 minutes?
Light rope 1 at both ends and rope 2 at one end simultaneously. When rope 1 finishes (30 min), light rope 2's other end. When rope 2 finishes = 45 minutes total.
On an island, every person is either a knight (always tells truth) or a knave (always lies). You meet two people, A and B. A says: 'At least one of us is a knave.' What are A and B?
A is a knight and B is a knave. If A were a knave, his statement ('at least one is a knave') would be true — a contradiction. So A is a knight telling the truth, which means B must be the knave.
What is the last digit of 7¹⁰⁰?
1. The last digits of powers of 7 cycle in groups of 4: 7, 9, 3, 1. Since 100 ÷ 4 = 25 exactly, the last digit is 1.

Crack the three-digit code. Each clue is exact: 682—one digit is correct and well placed; 614—one digit is correct but wrongly placed; 206—two digits are correct but wrongly placed; 738—no digit is correct; 780—one digit is correct but wrongly placed. What is the code?
042. Clue 738 removes 7, 3, and 8. Clue 780 then places 0 in the code but not third. Clues 682 and 614 eliminate 6 and put 2 third. Clue 206 puts 0 first, leaving 4 in the middle.

Four people must cross a narrow bridge at night with one torch. At most two can cross at a time, and anyone crossing must have the torch. They take 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes, and a pair walks at the slower person's pace. What is the shortest total time?
17 minutes: 1 and 2 cross (2), 1 returns (1), 5 and 10 cross (10), 2 returns (2), 1 and 2 cross (2).
You have a 4-minute hourglass and a 7-minute hourglass. How can you measure exactly 9 minutes?
Start both; turn the 4 over at minute 4 and the 7 at minute 7. When the 4 empties again (minute 8), turn the 7 over: its last minute of sand ends at minute 9.

A lion lies on Mondays, Tuesdays and Wednesdays and tells the truth on other days. A unicorn lies on Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays and tells the truth on other days. One day both say, 'Yesterday was one of my lying days.' What day is it?
Thursday. The lion could only say it on Monday or Thursday, and the unicorn only on Thursday or Sunday.

A census taker asks a mother the ages of her three children. 'Their ages multiply to 36,' she says, 'and add up to our house number.' He looks at the number and says he still can't tell. She adds, 'My oldest child loves dates.' What are the ages?
2, 2 and 9. Only 1 + 6 + 6 and 2 + 2 + 9 share a sum (13), and 'my oldest' rules out twins aged 6.
You have 25 horses and a track that races 5 at a time. There's no stopwatch, only the finishing order. What is the fewest races needed to find the three fastest horses?
7: five heats, one race of the five heat winners, then a final race of the five horses still in contention for 2nd and 3rd.

With two identical eggs and a 100-storey building, you must find the highest floor from which an egg survives a drop. A broken egg can't be reused. What is the fewest drops that guarantees the answer?
14. Drop the first egg from floors 14, 27, 39, 50 and so on (each jump one floor shorter), then test floor by floor with the second.

One of 1,000 juice bottles has gone bad. A test strip changes colour a day after touching even a drop of the bad juice, and one strip can take drops from many bottles. With just one day, what is the fewest strips you need to find the bad bottle?
10. Number the bottles in binary and give strip k a drop from every bottle whose k-th binary digit is 1. The strips that change spell out the bad bottle's number (2¹⁰ = 1,024).

Ten people stand in a line, each wearing a red or black hat, and each can see only the hats in front. Starting from the back, each says one colour, trying to name their own hat. If they agree on a plan beforehand, how many can be sure of being right?
9. The person at the back says 'red' if he sees an odd number of red hats, otherwise 'black'. Everyone else can then work out their own colour; only he takes a 50–50 chance.
Why can a bird sit safely on a single live power line?
Both its feet are at the same voltage, so no current flows through it.

To interrupt current flow after a fault is detected

Which ideal electronic component conducts current in the forward direction and blocks it in reverse?
An ideal diode. Real diodes also have leakage and breakdown limits.

How many equations make up Maxwell's equations?

Why is RMS used to measure AC voltage?
It gives the equivalent DC value producing the same heating effect
What limit does Shannon's noisy-channel coding theorem identify?
Channel capacity: the top data rate achievable with arbitrarily few errors.
What name was given to the 1880s–90s battle between Edison's direct current and the alternating current backed by Westinghouse and Tesla?
Your phone charger turns the wall's AC into the DC a battery needs. What is the circuit stage that does this called?
In three-phase power, how many degrees apart are the three voltage waves?
Why are you usually safe inside a metal-roofed car when lightning strikes it?
Its metal shell carries the current around you into the ground; tyres don't matter.
Saudi Arabia's grid runs at 60 Hz while its Gulf neighbours use 50 Hz. What kind of link lets them share power?
A back-to-back HVDC converter station (at Al-Fadhili).
At high frequencies, alternating current crowds near a wire's surface instead of using its whole thickness. What is this called?
On a 50 Hz grid, transformers hum at 100 Hz. What makes their iron core vibrate twice per cycle?
Magnetostriction: the iron changes shape slightly as it is magnetised.
What causes the crackling buzz you can hear near high-voltage power lines, especially in damp weather?
Corona discharge: the air around the wire becomes ionised.
Why do long undersea power cables usually carry direct current rather than alternating current?
With AC, the cable's capacitance draws large charging currents that waste its capacity.
Drop a strong magnet down a copper pipe and it falls in slow motion. Which law explains this?
Lenz's law: induced currents oppose the magnet's motion.
What does a power factor of 1 mean in an AC circuit?
Voltage and current are perfectly in step, so all the power does useful work.
How many stars are on the flag of the United States?
Which country's flag is a simple red circle on a white background?
Which country has a red maple leaf on its flag?
What is the name of the national flag of the United Kingdom?
What are the three colors on the French flag?
Which country’s flag has red above white, with a white crescent and five white stars in its upper-left corner?
Which country’s flag has a blue field, a Union Jack, and four red stars outlined in white representing the Southern Cross?
Green, White, Red vertical stripes — which European country?

What is the Arabic term for Islamic law derived from the Quran and Sunnah?
What is fiqh in Islamic legal terminology?
Fiqh is Islamic jurisprudence — the practical rulings derived by scholars from the sources of Sharia.
What are the four main sources of Islamic law (usul al-fiqh)?
The Quran, the Sunnah (Hadith), Ijma (scholarly consensus), and Qiyas (analogical reasoning).
What is a fatwa in Islamic law?
A formal legal opinion or ruling issued by a qualified Islamic scholar (mufti) on a religious or legal question.
What legal system is based on the Napoleonic Code and is used in many Arab countries?
Civil law (code law) system, as inherited from French or Egyptian civil codes.
What is the Arabic term for the fixed punishments prescribed by Islamic law for specific offenses?
Hudud (حدود) — the set of specific punishments for crimes like theft, slander, and highway robbery.
What is the Islamic legal principle of qisas?
Qisas is the principle of proportional retaliation ('an eye for an eye') in cases of murder or bodily harm, where the victim's family may choose retaliation, blood money, or forgiveness.
What is the Arabic legal term for a Muslim marriage contract?
Aqd al-nikah (عقد النكاح) — the marriage contract requiring offer, acceptance, two witnesses, and a dowry (mahr).
What is the mahr in Islamic marriage law?
A mandatory gift or payment made by the groom to the bride, which becomes her exclusive property.
What is the Arabic term for the waiting period a woman must observe after divorce or a husband's death before remarrying?
Iddah (عدة) — typically three menstrual cycles after divorce, or four months and ten days after a husband's death.
What is a waqf in Islamic law?
A waqf is a religious endowment — property donated for charitable, religious, or educational purposes, which cannot be sold or transferred.
What is the science of Islamic inheritance law called?
Ilm al-faraidh (علم الفرائض) — the science of prescribed inheritance shares defined in the Quran.
What does the term 'sovereignty' mean in international law?
The exclusive authority of a state to govern itself, make laws, and conduct affairs within its territory without interference from other states.
What does the Latin phrase 'presumption of innocence' mean in criminal law?
A defendant is considered innocent until proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt — the prosecution bears the burden of proof.
What country has the largest and most influential civil code in the Arab world, widely adopted by other nations?
Egypt — the Egyptian Civil Code (1949), drafted by Abd El-Razzak El-Sanhuri, was adopted as the basis for civil law in Iraq, Syria, Libya, Kuwait, and others.
What are the five categories of acts in Islamic law (ahkam al-khamsa)?
Wajib (obligatory), Mandub (recommended), Mubah (permissible), Makruh (discouraged), and Haram (forbidden).
What are the four major Sunni schools of Islamic jurisprudence (madhabs)?
The Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali schools, each named after its founding scholar.
What are the essential elements of a valid contract in most Arab civil law systems?
Offer and acceptance (meeting of minds), legal capacity of the parties, a lawful object, and a lawful cause (consideration).
What is the Arab League and what legal role does it play in the region?

Founded in 1945, the Arab League is a regional organization of Arab states that promotes cooperation and coordinates policy. It adopts resolutions and conventions, though its legal instruments are generally non-binding on member states without domestic ratification.
What constitutional provision is common to Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the UAE regarding the basis of their legal systems?
All three designate Islamic Sharia as a (or the) principal source of legislation in their constitutional documents.
What is ta'zir in Islamic criminal law?
Discretionary punishments imposed by a judge for offenses not covered by hudud or qisas, where the punishment type and severity is left to judicial discretion.
What is riba in Islamic law and how is it defined?

Riba (ربا) means any increase or excess charged over a loan principal — broadly interpreted as interest. It is prohibited in Islam. Islamic finance uses profit-sharing instruments (mudarabah, musharakah) to achieve similar economic outcomes without charging fixed interest.
What is the difference between talaq and khul' in Islamic divorce law?

Talaq is divorce initiated by the husband by pronouncing the divorce formula. Khul' is divorce initiated by the wife, who typically returns the mahr (dowry) to the husband in exchange for release from the marriage.
What is a sukuk in Islamic finance?

Sukuk are Islamic financial certificates representing ownership stakes in assets or projects — the Islamic equivalent of bonds. They generate returns through profit-sharing or rent from the underlying asset rather than interest payments.
What is the kafala (sponsorship) system common in Gulf states and how does it affect migrant workers?

The kafala system ties a migrant worker's legal residency and employment to a specific local sponsor (kafeel). Workers cannot change employers or leave the country without sponsor permission, creating dependency and vulnerability to exploitation. Several Gulf states have begun reforming or dismantling the system.
What is the principle of non-intervention in international law?

The principle that states are forbidden from intervening in the internal affairs of other sovereign states — enshrined in Article 2(1) of the UN Charter. It prohibits coercive interference in political, economic, or social matters.
What is the Cairo Declaration on Human Rights in Islam (1990)?

Adopted by the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), it affirms human rights but subordinates them to Islamic Sharia, offering an alternative framework to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It is criticized for limiting rights to what Sharia permits.
What is the burden of proof for hudud crimes in classical Islamic jurisprudence?

Extremely high — for example, zina (adultery/fornication) requires four male witnesses to the act itself. This effectively made enforcement rare in classical fiqh, with scholars arguing the strict standard was intended to limit actual punishment.
What is murabaha in Islamic finance and how is it used for home or car purchases?

Murabaha is a cost-plus financing arrangement: the bank buys an asset outright and resells it to the customer at a disclosed markup, payable in installments. This avoids interest while achieving similar financing outcomes.
What is the difference between a presidential and a parliamentary system of government?

In a presidential system (e.g. USA, Egypt), the executive is separate from the legislature and directly elected. In a parliamentary system (e.g. UK, Jordan), the executive (prime minister) is drawn from and accountable to the legislature.
What is the principle of jus cogens in international law?
Peremptory norms of international law from which no derogation is permitted — such as the prohibitions on genocide, slavery, and torture. They cannot be overridden by treaty.
What is the Islamic concept of wilaya in family law?

Wilaya is guardianship or protective authority — most commonly the male guardian's (wali) role in a woman's marriage, which classical fiqh requires for the marriage contract's validity. Contemporary Muslim-majority states vary widely in how strictly they apply this requirement.
What is ijara in Islamic finance?

Ijara is an Islamic leasing contract where a bank or financier buys an asset and leases it to the customer for an agreed rental, with ownership optionally transferring at the end. It is used for vehicle and equipment financing as an interest-free alternative.
What is the diya (blood money) system in Islamic law?

Diya is financial compensation paid to the victim or victim's family in cases of unintentional killing or bodily harm, as an alternative to qisas retaliation. Amounts vary by injury type and are still applied in several Muslim-majority legal systems.
What is the International Court of Justice (ICJ) and what types of cases does it hear?

The principal judicial organ of the UN, based in The Hague. It settles legal disputes between states (contentious cases) and gives advisory opinions on legal questions referred by UN organs. Only states — not individuals — can be parties to contentious cases.
What is the Arab Charter on Human Rights?

A human rights instrument adopted by the Arab League in 2004, entering into force in 2008. It guarantees civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights, but is criticized for allowing derogation on national security grounds and for not fully aligning with international standards.
What is the role of the Constitutional Court in Egypt's legal system?

Egypt's Supreme Constitutional Court has exclusive jurisdiction over the constitutionality of legislation, interprets legislative texts referred to it, and settles jurisdictional conflicts between courts. Its rulings are final and binding on all state organs.
What is the Wage Protection System (WPS) used in UAE and Saudi Arabia?

An electronic salary monitoring system that requires employers to pay workers' wages through approved financial channels on time. Compliance is tracked by authorities, and non-paying employers face fines, work permit bans, or criminal prosecution.
What is ijtihad in Islamic law and why was it historically controversial?

Ijtihad is independent legal reasoning to derive new rulings on matters not explicitly addressed in the Quran or Sunnah. It became controversial after classical scholars declared 'the closing of the gate of ijtihad' — suggesting most major legal questions had been settled — though this view is contested and modern reformists strongly advocate reopening ijtihad.
What is arbitration and why is it commonly used in international commercial contracts in the Middle East?

Arbitration is a private dispute resolution process where parties agree to submit disputes to one or more arbitrators whose decision (award) is binding. In international trade, it is preferred over national courts because it is neutral, confidential, and awards are enforceable internationally under the New York Convention (1958).
What is the difference between a crime and a tort in most Arab civil law systems?

A crime is a wrong against society prosecuted by the state, resulting in criminal penalties (imprisonment, fines). A tort (civil wrong) is a wrong against an individual that gives rise to a private civil action for compensation. The same act can constitute both a crime and a tort simultaneously.
What is the difference between ownership and possession in Arab civil law?

Ownership (milkiyya) is the full legal right to use, enjoy, and dispose of property. Possession (hiyaza) is the physical control of property, which may exist without ownership (e.g. a tenant possesses but doesn't own). Possession can give rise to certain legal protections even without full title.
How do dual legal systems (mixed sharia-civil law) function in countries like Egypt, Jordan, and Kuwait?

These countries apply civil law codes (French-derived) for commercial and criminal matters while applying Sharia in personal status law (marriage, divorce, inheritance, guardianship). Separate courts (personal status or sharia courts) handle family matters, while civil and criminal courts handle the rest. Integration is complex — Sharia principles often inform constitutional interpretation even in the civil domain.
What is the doctrine of maslaha (public interest) in Islamic jurisprudence and how has it been used in legal reform?

Maslaha holds that rulings may be derived or reformed to serve the public good, even if not explicitly derived from Quran or Sunnah texts, provided they do not contradict established principles. Reformist scholars use it to argue for updating Islamic law on issues like women's rights, banking, and criminal penalties to fit modern contexts.
What is the Responsibility to Protect (R2P) doctrine and how has it been applied in the Arab world?

R2P holds that states have a primary responsibility to protect their populations from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing, and crimes against humanity. When a state fails, the international community may intervene. It was controversially invoked for the 2011 NATO intervention in Libya (UNSC Resolution 1973), raising debates about its limits and potential for misuse.
What is the concept of shura in Islamic political theory and how do Gulf states incorporate it into governance?

Shura is the principle of consultation — rulers should consult with advisors or representatives before making decisions. Gulf states incorporate it through consultative councils (like Saudi Arabia's Majlis al-Shura or Qatar's Majlis) that advise the ruler but lack full legislative power, representing a partial institutionalization of shura principles.
What is the role of a Sharia Supervisory Board in Islamic banking?

A Sharia Supervisory Board is a panel of qualified Islamic scholars who review and certify that a bank's financial products, contracts, and operations comply with Sharia principles. They issue fatwas on products and audit transactions. Their independence and consistency across institutions remains a subject of debate in Islamic finance governance.
What are the Rome Statute and the International Criminal Court (ICC), and why have some Arab states not ratified them?

The Rome Statute (1998) established the ICC, the first permanent international criminal court with jurisdiction over genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Many Arab states have not ratified it due to concerns about sovereignty, potential politically motivated prosecutions, and the ICC's previous focus on African and Middle Eastern situations. What class of drugs kills or inhibits bacteria?

What is a diuretic and what condition is it commonly used to treat?
A drug that increases urine production, commonly used to treat hypertension (high blood pressure) and edema (fluid retention).
What class of drugs lowers blood glucose levels and is used to treat diabetes?
Antidiabetic drugs — including insulin (injected) and oral hypoglycemics like metformin.
What does the term 'half-life' of a drug mean?
The time it takes for the concentration of a drug in the body to decrease by half. It determines how frequently a drug must be dosed.
What is the difference between a side effect and an adverse drug reaction?

A side effect is any secondary, usually unintended effect of a drug at therapeutic doses. An adverse drug reaction (ADR) is a harmful, unintended response at normal doses — a subset of side effects that causes harm.
What is the mechanism of action of NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) like ibuprofen?
NSAIDs inhibit the enzyme cyclooxygenase (COX), which reduces prostaglandin synthesis — thereby decreasing inflammation, pain, and fever.
What does 'oral bioavailability' of a drug mean?

The fraction of an orally administered drug that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged. A drug with 100% bioavailability is fully absorbed; low bioavailability means much is destroyed before reaching the bloodstream.
What are statins and what condition do they treat?

Statins (e.g. atorvastatin, simvastatin) are drugs that inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, reducing cholesterol synthesis in the liver. They treat hypercholesterolemia (high cholesterol) and reduce cardiovascular risk.
What are beta-blockers and what conditions are they used for?
Drugs that block beta-adrenergic receptors, slowing the heart rate and reducing blood pressure. Used for hypertension, angina, heart failure, and arrhythmias (e.g. atenolol, metoprolol).
What is a contraindication in pharmacology?

A specific situation or condition in which a drug should NOT be used because it may be harmful to the patient — for example, aspirin is contraindicated in children with viral infections (Reye's syndrome risk).
What is the difference between a generic drug and a branded drug?

A branded drug is the original patented formulation. A generic drug contains the same active ingredient, same dose, same route, and meets bioequivalence standards — but is sold under its chemical name at lower cost once the patent expires.
What are the four pharmacokinetic processes described by ADME?
Absorption (drug enters circulation), Distribution (drug spreads to tissues), Metabolism (drug is chemically altered, mainly by liver), and Excretion (drug is eliminated, mainly by kidneys).
What is a drug-drug interaction and give one clinically important example?

When one drug affects the activity of another. Example: Warfarin (blood thinner) combined with aspirin increases bleeding risk because both inhibit clotting through different mechanisms — dose adjustment and monitoring are required.
What is antibiotic resistance and how does it develop?

The ability of bacteria to survive and grow despite antibiotic treatment. It develops when bacteria acquire mutations or resistance genes — accelerated by overuse, incomplete courses, and use in livestock. Resistant bacteria spread, making infections harder to treat.
What are ACE inhibitors and what do they treat?

Drugs that block the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), preventing conversion of angiotensin I to the vasoconstrictor angiotensin II. They lower blood pressure and are first-line for hypertension and heart failure (e.g. lisinopril, enalapril).
What is the difference between an agonist and an antagonist in pharmacology?
An agonist binds to a receptor and activates it, producing a biological response. An antagonist binds to the receptor but does NOT activate it — it blocks agonists from binding, reducing a response.
What is the therapeutic index of a drug?

The ratio between the toxic dose and the effective dose (TD50/ED50). A wide therapeutic index means a drug is relatively safe; a narrow therapeutic index (e.g. warfarin, lithium, digoxin) means small dose changes can cause toxicity or loss of effect.
What is the mechanism of action of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) like omeprazole?
PPIs irreversibly block the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (proton pump) in gastric parietal cells, stopping acid secretion. They treat peptic ulcers, GERD, and H. pylori infections.
What is the mechanism of action of penicillin-class antibiotics?

Penicillins inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis by blocking transpeptidase enzymes (penicillin-binding proteins), preventing cross-linking of peptidoglycan chains. This weakens the cell wall, causing the bacterium to burst (lyse).
What is the 'first-pass effect' and which drugs are most affected by it?

When an orally administered drug is absorbed through the gut and passes through the portal vein to the liver before reaching systemic circulation, much of it is metabolized — reducing bioavailability. Highly metabolized drugs like morphine, nitroglycerin, and lidocaine show significant first-pass effects and may need higher oral doses or alternative routes.
What are SSRIs and what are they primarily used to treat?

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors block reuptake of serotonin in synapses, increasing serotonin availability. They are the first-line treatment for depression and anxiety disorders (e.g. fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram).
What is the WHO's ATC (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical) classification system?

A system for classifying drugs by the organ or body system they act on and their therapeutic, pharmacological, and chemical properties — organized in five levels. It is used globally for drug utilization research and comparison.
What is heparin and how does it work as an anticoagulant?

Heparin is an injectable anticoagulant that activates antithrombin III, which then rapidly inactivates thrombin and factor Xa — key enzymes in the clotting cascade. Used to prevent and treat blood clots (DVT, pulmonary embolism).
What is receptor downregulation and what clinical problem can it cause?

When a receptor is chronically activated (by an agonist drug), the cell reduces the number of available receptors. This causes drug tolerance — the same dose produces a weaker effect over time, requiring dose escalation. It is a major issue with opioids and beta-agonists in asthma.
What is volume of distribution (Vd) and what does a high Vd indicate?

Vd is a theoretical volume relating the total amount of drug in the body to its plasma concentration (Vd = total drug / plasma concentration). A high Vd means the drug distributes extensively into tissues and is not confined to plasma — making it harder to remove by dialysis. Lipophilic drugs (e.g. chloroquine, amiodarone) have very high Vd values.
What is the difference between bactericidal and bacteriostatic antibiotics and does it matter clinically?

Bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria (e.g. penicillins, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides); bacteriostatic antibiotics inhibit growth, relying on immune clearance (e.g. tetracyclines, macrolides, sulfonamides). In immunocompromised patients or endocarditis, bactericidal drugs are preferred because the immune system cannot finish the job.
What is Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) in drug safety?

A rare but life-threatening hypersensitivity reaction causing blistering and peeling of skin and mucous membranes. Commonly triggered by drugs including carbamazepine, allopurinol, lamotrigine, sulfonamides, and NSAIDs. It requires immediate discontinuation of the offending drug and intensive supportive care.
What is the mechanism of action of metformin in type 2 diabetes?

Metformin primarily activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) in the liver, inhibiting gluconeogenesis (glucose production) and reducing hepatic glucose output. It also improves insulin sensitivity in peripheral tissues. It does not cause hypoglycemia and is weight-neutral.
What is the difference between Phase I and Phase II drug metabolism?

Phase I reactions (mainly by CYP450 enzymes in liver) introduce or unmask functional groups (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) — often activating prodrugs or making drugs more polar. Phase II reactions conjugate the drug or Phase I metabolite with endogenous molecules (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation) to make them more water-soluble for excretion.
What is the mechanism of warfarin and why does it require careful monitoring?

Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, preventing regeneration of vitamin K — essential for producing clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X. Its effect is measured by INR. It has a narrow therapeutic index, is affected by diet (vitamin K foods) and many drug interactions (especially CYP2C9 inhibitors/inducers), requiring regular dose adjustment.
What is the difference between tolerance, dependence, and addiction in the context of opioid drugs?

Tolerance: reduced drug effect with repeated use, requiring higher doses. Physical dependence: physiological adaptation where abrupt cessation causes withdrawal syndrome. Addiction: compulsive drug-seeking behavior despite harmful consequences — a neurological disease. All three can coexist; tolerance and dependence can occur without addiction.
What is the difference between drug toxicity and drug allergy?

Drug toxicity is a dose-dependent, pharmacologically predictable harmful effect (e.g. acetaminophen overdose causing liver failure). Drug allergy is an immune-mediated reaction (hypersensitivity) that can occur at any dose, is unpredictable from pharmacology, and requires prior sensitization — ranging from mild rash to life-threatening anaphylaxis.
What is the mechanism of aminoglycoside antibiotics and what is their main toxicity?

Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin) irreversibly bind the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA and production of faulty proteins — killing bacteria. Their main toxicities are nephrotoxicity (kidney damage) and ototoxicity (hearing/balance damage), which are dose-related and cumulative.
What is the concept of 'therapeutic drug monitoring' (TDM) and which drug classes benefit most?

TDM is the practice of measuring drug concentrations in blood to optimize dosing. Most useful for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index and high inter-patient variability: aminoglycosides, vancomycin, lithium, phenytoin, digoxin, cyclosporine, and tacrolimus.
What is pharmacogenomics and how can CYP2D6 polymorphisms affect drug therapy?

Pharmacogenomics studies how genetic variation affects drug response. CYP2D6 metabolizes ~25% of drugs (codeine, tamoxifen, many antidepressants). Poor metabolizers accumulate drug, risking toxicity; ultra-rapid metabolizers clear it too fast, losing efficacy. Codeine in ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolizers converts to dangerous morphine levels — an FDA-labeled risk.
What is the difference between zero-order and first-order drug elimination kinetics?

First-order kinetics: a constant fraction of drug is eliminated per unit time (most drugs) — concentration-time curve is exponential. Zero-order kinetics: a constant amount is eliminated per unit time regardless of concentration (e.g. ethanol, phenytoin at high doses) — because eliminating enzymes are saturated. Zero-order kinetics causes disproportionate toxicity with dose escalation.
What are the four phases of clinical drug trials?

Phase I: safety, tolerability, PK/PD in small healthy volunteers. Phase II: efficacy and safety in small patient populations, dose-finding. Phase III: large randomized controlled trials confirming efficacy and safety vs. placebo/standard care — required for regulatory approval. Phase IV: post-marketing surveillance for long-term or rare adverse effects.
What is the concept of 'targeted therapy' in oncology and how do tyrosine kinase inhibitors work?

Targeted therapy attacks specific molecular abnormalities in cancer cells rather than killing all rapidly dividing cells. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) like imatinib (Gleevec) block overactive kinase enzymes (e.g. BCR-ABL in CML) that drive cancer cell proliferation. They are more selective and often have fewer side effects than traditional chemotherapy.
What are the main molecular mechanisms by which bacteria develop antibiotic resistance?

1. Enzymatic inactivation (e.g. beta-lactamases destroying penicillins). 2. Target modification (altered penicillin-binding proteins in MRSA). 3. Efflux pumps (actively expelling antibiotic from cell). 4. Reduced permeability (decreased outer membrane porins). 5. Target bypass (alternative metabolic pathways). Resistance genes can transfer between bacteria via plasmids (horizontal gene transfer).
What is the difference between a competitive reversible antagonist and a non-competitive irreversible antagonist?

A competitive reversible antagonist competes with the agonist for the same binding site — its effect can be overcome by increasing agonist concentration (the dose-response curve shifts right but maximum effect is maintained). A non-competitive/irreversible antagonist binds covalently or at an allosteric site, and its effect cannot be overcome by more agonist — maximum effect is reduced even at high agonist doses.
What is 'prodrug design' and give a clinically important example?

A prodrug is an inactive compound that is converted in the body to its active form. Prodrug design improves bioavailability, stability, or reduces toxicity. Example: Enalapril is an ester prodrug of enalaprilat — the active ACE inhibitor — because enalaprilat is poorly absorbed orally but enalapril's ester is absorbed well and hydrolyzed to enalaprilat after absorption.
What are monoclonal antibodies and how are they used as drugs?

Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are laboratory-produced antibodies that bind a specific target (antigen) with high precision. As drugs, they can block disease-causing proteins (e.g. trastuzumab blocks HER2 in breast cancer; adalimumab blocks TNF-α in rheumatoid arthritis; rituximab depletes CD20-positive B cells in lymphoma). They often have suffix -mab in their name.
What is the concept of 'mechanism-based inhibition' (suicide inhibition) of CYP450 enzymes?

Some drugs are metabolized by CYP450 enzymes into reactive intermediates that permanently inactivate the enzyme — 'committing suicide.' This causes irreversible drug interactions lasting until new enzyme is synthesized (days–weeks). Examples: erythromycin (CYP3A4), isoniazid (CYP2E1), grapefruit furanocoumarins (CYP3A4 in gut wall). Drug levels of CYP3A4 substrates can rise dramatically when grapefruit is consumed.
What is 'biopharmaceutics classification system' (BCS) and how does it guide drug formulation?

The BCS classifies drugs by aqueous solubility and intestinal permeability into 4 classes: I (high solubility, high permeability — ideal), II (low solubility, high permeability — formulation key to improving dissolution), III (high solubility, low permeability — absorption enhancement needed), IV (low solubility, low permeability — most challenging). BCS guides whether modified-release or special delivery systems are needed for adequate bioavailability.
What is the mechanism of action of checkpoint inhibitors in cancer immunotherapy?

Tumor cells evade immune destruction by expressing inhibitory checkpoint proteins (PD-L1, CTLA-4) that suppress T-cell activity. Checkpoint inhibitors (e.g. nivolumab, pembrolizumab block PD-1; ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4) remove these brakes, allowing T cells to recognize and kill cancer cells. This can cause immune-related adverse effects in normal tissues.
What are lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and why were they critical to mRNA vaccine delivery?

Lipid nanoparticles are tiny spherical vesicles made of lipids that encapsulate and protect mRNA from degradation and facilitate its delivery into cells. They fuse with cell membranes, releasing mRNA into the cytoplasm. This technology, developed over decades, was essential for COVID-19 mRNA vaccines (Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna) — solving the major challenge that naked mRNA is rapidly degraded in the body.
What is the difference between pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic drug tolerance?

Pharmacokinetic tolerance: the body metabolizes or excretes the drug faster over time (enzyme induction), reducing plasma levels after the same dose. Pharmacodynamic tolerance: the drug concentration is unchanged but the target response is reduced — via receptor downregulation, desensitization, or compensatory physiological changes. Both mechanisms can contribute simultaneously.
What is PBPK (physiologically based pharmacokinetic) modelling and what is its value in drug development?

PBPK models use mathematical equations representing actual organ volumes, blood flows, and biochemical processes to simulate drug distribution and elimination throughout the whole body. They can predict drug behavior in special populations (children, pregnant women, patients with renal/hepatic impairment) without exposing them to the drug — reducing costly animal studies and informing regulatory submissions for dose adjustment recommendations.

Which reply asks whether a friend wants advice before giving it? A: “Would you prefer that I listen, or would ideas be useful?” B: “Here is what you must do.”
A — It lets the friend state what kind of support they want.
You want to discuss an important issue. Which opener checks timing? A: “We are discussing this now, whatever you are doing.” B: “Is now a good time to talk for ten minutes?”
B — It asks whether the other person is available.

A short message seems rude to you. Which response checks intent rather than assuming it? A: “You wrote “fine” because you wanted to insult me.” B: “When you wrote “fine,” did you mean the plan works for you?”
B — It treats the interpretation as a question, not a fact.

Which response acknowledges a feeling without necessarily agreeing with the person’s interpretation of events? A: “If I disagree with your explanation, your feelings cannot be real.” B: “I can hear that you felt left out; tell me more.”
B — Acknowledging a reported feeling is different from endorsing every factual claim.

You remember an agreement differently. Which reply separates your memory from certainty? A: “I remember Tuesday, but I may be mistaken. Can we check the message?” B: “My memory is perfect, so you must be lying.”
A — It allows error and proposes checking shared evidence.
Which question is open-ended rather than answerable only with yes or no? A: “Do you want to change the plan?” B: “What part of the plan would you like to change?”
B — It asks for details, not just confirmation.
A friend declines an invitation. Which reply accepts the refusal without pressure? A: “Thanks for letting me know. Perhaps another time.” B: “If you cared about me, you would come.”
A — It does not make affection conditional on accepting the invitation.

Before posting a photograph that clearly shows your friend, which action seeks their permission? A: “Assume that posing for the photo permits every future use.” B: “Ask whether they are comfortable with that photo being posted.”
B — Being photographed and agreeing to publication are separate choices.

A friend wants to borrow an item you do not lend out. Which reply states the boundary without attacking them? A: “I do not lend this item, but I can help you find another option.” B: “Sorry, I can't lend it. People like you tend to be careless with things.”
A — It states the rule without judging the friend’s character.
Psychologist John Gottman named four habits in arguments that predict a relationship breaking down, the 'Four Horsemen'. What are they?

Your friend says a joke about them is unwelcome. Which reply responds to the stated limit rather than debating their right to have it? A: “You must learn to enjoy it because I find it funny.” B: “I hear you. I will stop making that joke about you.”
B — It addresses the behavior the friend asked to stop.
What name is given to a sentence like 'I feel worried when plans change at the last minute', which starts from your own feelings instead of blaming?
Which American psychologist, founder of person-centred therapy, co-wrote the 1957 paper that named 'active listening'?

Two housemates disagree about guests. Which proposal creates a shared rule rather than a unilateral demand? A: “Only my preferences count because I mentioned the problem first.” B: “Let us agree on notice, visiting hours and how either of us can raise a concern.”
B — It invites both people to define the agreement.

Which statement distinguishes a request from a demand by allowing the other person to decline? A: “Would you be willing to help Saturday? It is okay if you cannot.” B: “Would you be willing to help Saturday? I'll be really hurt if you say no.”
A — It leaves a genuine option to decline; B adds guilt pressure.
An agreed apology format has three parts: name your action, acknowledge its effect, and offer a repair. “I interrupted twice, so you could not finish. I am sorry.” Which part is still missing?
A repair offer, such as: “Please finish; I will listen without interrupting.”
Which four-pane model (open, blind, hidden and unknown) maps what you and other people know about you?

Which sentence stays with the current disagreement rather than introducing an unrelated past complaint? A: “This reminds me of everything you did wrong last year.” B: “Let us first decide how to divide tonight’s cleanup.”
B — It keeps the immediate problem defined.
“I meant the comment as a joke.” “I felt embarrassed when you said it in front of the group.” Which statement describes intent, and which describes reported impact?
The first describes intent; the second reports impact. They can both be true.
Maya suggests a café because she wants somewhere quiet. Sam suggests a park because he needs a free outing. Before comparing venues, what two underlying needs should their plan address?
A quiet setting and no cost; the café and park are proposed solutions, not the underlying needs.
Anthropologist Robin Dunbar proposed a rough limit on how many stable relationships one person can keep up. About how many?
The word for manipulating someone until they doubt their own memory comes from the title of which 1938 play, later a 1944 film?

Asking someone for a small favour can make them like you more. Which American founding father described winning over a rival by borrowing a rare book from him?
Classify these as observation, interpretation, or request: 1 “We spoke for five minutes.” 2 “You wanted to avoid me.” 3 “Could we set aside half an hour tomorrow?”
What did John Gottman call any joke, smile or 'let's take a break' that stops an argument from spiralling?

Both friends know a train takes 40 minutes and a bus takes 70. One values saving time; the other values the bus's lower fare. Is the remaining disagreement about the travel-time facts or about priorities?
Priorities: they agree on the times but weigh time and cost differently.
Marshall Rosenberg's 'Nonviolent Communication' is built on four components. Name them.
A popular rule says only 7% of a message's meaning comes from words. What did Albert Mehrabian, whose experiments it comes from, say about it?

A 1950 study of student housing by Festinger, Schachter and Back found that friendships depended heavily on which simple factor?
Physical closeness: people mostly befriended their nearest neighbours.
Arthur Aron's 1997 study built closeness between strangers using a set of how many increasingly personal questions?

A friend permits you to send one photograph to Noor by private message, without reposting it. Which action stays within that permission? A: Send it to Noor privately. B: Add it to a private group that includes Noor. C: Post it without naming the friend.
A. The permission specifies one recipient and a private message; a group or unnamed post extends the audience.

The group agreed: book only after all three people explicitly confirm both the date and venue. Noor confirms Friday at Café X; Sam confirms Friday but asks about another venue; Lina has not replied. What confirmations are still needed?
Sam must confirm the venue, and Lina must confirm both date and venue. Any changed plan needs renewed confirmation from everyone.
A chat shows “read at 2:10.” By 2:30 there is no reply. Name one observation the record supports and one conclusion about motive it does not establish.
Observation: no reply appears by 2:30. Not established: that the person is deliberately ignoring or upsetting the sender.

Metal conducts heat away from your hand much faster than wood, even though both begin at the same temperature.

What is the term for the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another?

The energy required to raise the temperature of one unit mass of the substance by one degree.
What is the temperature of absolute zero in Celsius?

Archimedes. The bathtub account is a traditional story, not a contemporary experimental record.

The energy of a photon to its frequency

Which field do elementary particles such as electrons interact with to acquire their rest masses in the Standard Model?
The Higgs field. The Higgs boson is an excitation of that field.
According to special relativity, how does an observer measure the ticking rate of a clock moving rapidly relative to them?
The moving clock ticks more slowly than clocks at rest in the observer's frame. This is relative time dilation, not a change in how the traveler experiences their own clock.

What is the SI unit of mechanical pressure?
The pascal (Pa), equal to one newton per square metre.
Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
Arteries. Pulmonary arteries are an exception to the usual oxygen-rich pattern, but they still carry blood away from the heart.

About 400–700 nanometres; the limits of human vision vary and are not sharp cutoffs.

To carry oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues
Which optical processes in raindrops produce a primary rainbow?
Refraction and dispersion as light enters and leaves, with one internal reflection inside each drop.

Why does a clear daytime sky usually appear blue?
Rayleigh scattering: molecules in the atmosphere scatter shorter visible wavelengths more strongly than longer ones.
On a freezing night, water vapour turns straight into frost on a window without becoming liquid first. What is this change of state called?
What fundamental connection does Noether's theorem make in physics?
Every continuous symmetry of a system's action corresponds to a conservation law; for example, time-translation symmetry gives conservation of energy.
What equation gives the de Broglie wavelength of a particle?
λ = h/p, where h is Planck's constant and p is the particle's momentum.
What gauge symmetry group underlies the Standard Model of particle physics?
SU(3)C × SU(2)L × U(1)Y, corresponding to the strong and electroweak interactions before symmetry breaking.
A uniformly accelerating observer perceives the inertial vacuum as a thermal bath, with temperature proportional to the observer's acceleration.
A closed system experiences no net external force. Which quantity is conserved: total momentum or each object's speed?
Total momentum. Individual objects can change speed while exchanging momentum internally.
What does the Pauli Exclusion Principle state?
No two fermions in the same quantum system can have the same quantum state simultaneously
What is the significance of the triple point of a substance?
The unique temperature and pressure at which the three phases (solid, liquid, gas) coexist in equilibrium
What is the principle of superposition in quantum mechanics?
If quantum states are allowed, an appropriate linear combination of them is also an allowed state. Measurement outcome probabilities depend on the combination's amplitudes.
What expected effect did the Michelson–Morley experiment fail to detect?
The expected light-speed difference caused by Earth's motion through a stationary luminiferous ether—the proposed ether wind.

How are the frequency f and period T of a repeating wave related?
They are reciprocals: f = 1/T. A longer period therefore means a lower frequency.

What is the difference between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion?
Fission splits a heavy nucleus into smaller ones (used in nuclear reactors); fusion merges light nuclei into heavier ones (powers the Sun). Both release enormous energy.
Quantum objects (electrons, photons) exhibit both wave-like and particle-like behaviour depending on how they are observed. The double-slit experiment demonstrates this duality.
Why was the photoelectric effect important to the development of quantum theory?
Electron emission depends on a threshold light frequency. Einstein explained it using light quanta with energy E=hf, where classical wave theory alone could not explain the observations.
Can measurements of entangled particles be used to send a controllable message faster than light?
No. Entanglement produces nonclassical correlations, but comparing outcomes still requires ordinary communication subject to the light-speed limit.
Which bosons mediate the electromagnetic, weak, and strong interactions in the Standard Model?
The photon mediates electromagnetism, W and Z bosons the weak interaction, and gluons the strong interaction. The Higgs boson is a separate scalar particle.
What is the key difference between special and general relativity in their treatment of spacetime and gravity?
Special relativity describes physics in flat spacetime, including accelerated motion. General relativity describes gravity through curved spacetime shaped by mass-energy.
What characterizes a Bose–Einstein condensate in a dilute gas cooled to extremely low temperature?
A macroscopic fraction of the bosons occupies the same lowest-energy quantum state. Bosons have integer spin.
On a hot desert road, a mirage looks just like a shimmering pool of water. What are you really seeing in that 'pool'?
An image of the sky: hot air near the ground bends (refracts) light from the sky up towards your eyes.
A plain clay water jar keeps water cool, but a glazed one doesn't. Why?
The glaze seals the pores, so no water seeps out to evaporate, and evaporation is what carries the heat away.
You see a lightning flash and count the seconds until the thunder. Roughly how many seconds of delay mean the storm is 1 km away?
About 3 seconds: sound travels roughly 340 metres per second, while the light arrives almost instantly.
On the Moon in 1971, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather at the same moment. Which hit the ground first?
Neither: they landed together, because there is no air resistance on the Moon.
A spinning figure skater pulls in her arms and suddenly spins much faster. Which conservation law explains this?
Why do rice and pasta take longer to cook high up in the mountains?
Lower air pressure lowers water's boiling point, so the water boils at a cooler temperature.
Gravity at the height of the International Space Station is still about 90% as strong as on the ground. So why do astronauts such as the UAE's Sultan Al Neyadi float there?
The station and everyone in it are in continuous free fall around Earth.
Clocks on GPS satellites gain about 38 microseconds a day compared with clocks on the ground. Which theory predicts this drift, which must be corrected for GPS to work?
Einstein's relativity (mostly general relativity: clocks tick faster where gravity is weaker).
The water around some nuclear reactor cores glows an eerie blue. What is this light called?
Cherenkov radiation, given off when charged particles move faster than light can travel in water.
In the Sun's core, protons rarely have enough energy to overcome their mutual repulsion, yet they still fuse. Which quantum effect makes this possible?

In 1676, by timing the eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io, which Danish astronomer showed that light does not travel instantly?
Which French thinker coined the term sociology in the nineteenth century?

The word 'democracy' comes from two Greek words. What does it literally mean?
Which oil organisation was founded in Baghdad in 1960 by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela?

Queuing in line or shaking hands when you meet someone are examples of unwritten rules called what?
In a competitive market, what do economists call the price at which supply equals demand?
In what year was the United Nations founded?
Children learn their society's values, customs and roles from family, school and friends. What is this lifelong process called?
What is the principle of understanding a culture by its own standards, rather than judging it by yours, called?
In Max Weber's sociology, is an ideal type a model of moral perfection or an analytical comparison tool?
An analytical comparison tool, not a moral ideal.
Which branch of economics studies the economy as a whole: national output, unemployment and the overall price level?
What do we call a vote in which all citizens decide directly on a single question, such as a new constitution?
What does Durkheim's concept of anomie describe?
A weakening or breakdown of social norms and regulation, especially during rapid change.
Which hypothesis, named after two American linguists, proposes that the language you speak can shape how you think?
What idea is commonly associated with Adam Smith's metaphor of an invisible hand?
Self-interest in markets can unintentionally benefit society.
In which kind of state is power shared between a national government and regions, as in the USA or Germany?

What do economists call a side effect, like factory pollution, that falls on people outside the deal?

What relationship does democratic peace theory propose between established liberal democracies?
That they rarely, if ever, go to war with each other.
Which term did Stanley Cohen use for a disproportionate public reaction to a perceived threat to social values?
Moral panic; his classic study examined reactions to the Mods and Rockers in Britain.
Which field, linked to Kahneman and Tversky, uses psychology to explain why people's economic choices are often not 'rational'?
According to the most widely accepted model, on which continent did modern humans (Homo sapiens) first evolve?
In Gramsci's theory, how does hegemony help dominant groups maintain power?
By winning consent through culture and ideas, not just force.
Which French thinker coined 'biopower' for the way modern states manage their populations' health, births and lives?
What is the main warning of the Lucas critique for evaluating economic policy?
Past statistical patterns may break when a new policy changes expectations.
Which British sociologist's 'structuration theory' says social structures and individual actions constantly shape each other?
Voters hand power to politicians who may then pursue their own interests. Which 'problem' from economics and political science describes this?
Which American anthropologist popularised 'thick description' in 1973, using the difference between a wink and an involuntary twitch?
Which sociologist's world-systems theory divides countries into a core, a semi-periphery and a periphery?
Which economist's 1817 theory of 'comparative advantage' explains why countries gain by specialising and trading?
The QWERTY keyboard layout outlived the typewriters it was designed for. Which 'history matters' concept is it a classic example of?
Which Palestinian-American scholar's 1978 book 'Orientalism' became a founding text of post-colonial studies?
What role does aggregate demand play in Keynesian explanations of a recession?
Too little total spending, which cuts output and jobs.
Which Iraqi sociologist (1913–1995) wrote 'A Study into the Nature of Iraqi Society', contrasting Bedouin and urban ways of life?

Which German sociologist published 'Risk Society' in 1986, the year of the Chernobyl disaster?
What does CPU stand for and what does it do?
Central Processing Unit: the chip that carries out the computer's instructions.
What is the difference between RAM and ROM?
RAM is temporary working memory, wiped when power goes off; ROM keeps its contents permanently.
Why do computers store information as 0s and 1s?
Because electronic circuits can reliably tell two states apart, such as low and high voltage, which stand for 0 and 1.
What is the basic distinction between compilation and interpretation?
Compiling translates the program into another form first; interpreting runs it directly. Many systems mix both.
What does HTTP stand for and what is it used for?
HyperText Transfer Protocol: the rules browsers and servers use to exchange web pages.
What is the difference between a process and a thread?
A process has its own memory; threads run inside a process and share it.
